top_articles.title: Fast, reliable A2UI, with swappable inference formats
top_articles.summary: A2UI now supports swappable inference formats, introducing A2UI Express which uses up to 3x fewer tokens and cuts latency by compiling compact Python-style syntax into standard A2UI JSON via Agent SDKs. Developers can also use controlled generation with TypeSafe's Jev system-decision models to render known-shape screens in under 300 ms while smaller models stream text. These updates require no changes to frontend renderers or component catalogs, offering flexible performance levers for generative UI development across Python, TypeScript, and Dart.

top_articles.title: Catch Go bugs that fuzzing misses with Gemini and a constraint solver
top_articles.summary: How pairing Go's surviving compiler bounds-check traps with Gemini 4 Argon and the Z3 constraint solver catches latent out-of-bounds panics in Go code and uncovers a slice-capacity blind spot in go test -fuzz.

top_articles.title: On-Device Speech Recognition and Text-to-Speech in Google AI Edge Gallery
top_articles.summary: Google AI Edge Gallery now supports on-device, offline Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Text-to-Speech (TTS) capabilities for building developer-friendly voice applications. Developers can leverage ML Kit for optimized Android performance, or use MediaPipe Tasks and LiteRT for cross-platform open-weight model integration. This local pipeline seamlessly pairs lightweight speech models with on-device small language models like Gemini Nano and Gemma 4 to enable real-time streaming transcription and low-latency synthesis.

top_articles.title: Integrating TorchTPU into TorchTitan and Optimizing Models for TPU
top_articles.summary: TorchTPU integrates a native torch.device("tpu") backend directly into PyTorch, allowing developers to train large-scale models on Google Cloud TPUs without rewriting code in JAX. The TorchTitan TPU fork enhances this with production-grade scaling primitives like SimpleFSDP, Graph Trainer, and custom Pallas kernels that achieve high Model Flops Utilization (MFU) across dense and MoE architectures. Developers can leverage these battle-tested optimization playbooks, recipes, and the Hugging Face modeling backend to efficiently scale their own workloads on TPU infrastructure.

Backend.title: TermSSH: SSH, Files, Monitoring, and Databases in One Browser Workspace
Backend.summary:
TermSSH: SSH, Files, Monitoring, and Databases in One Browser Workspace

If you manage remote servers, your workflow probably looks something like this:

  1. Open an SSH session.
  2. Check the application service.
  3. Read the logs.
  4. Edit a configuration file.
  5. Inspect resource usage.
  6. Open a database client.
  7. Repeat on staging.

TermSSH brings these tasks into a shared browser workspace, using the SSH access you already have.

The website calls the application Secure Console, and its public walkthrough covers much more than an embedded terminal.

What’s inside?

Area Advertised capabilities
SSH terminal Full browser shell, keyboard and colour support, sessions that continue across pages, automatic reconnection
Server connections Saved servers and trusted host-key checking before credentials are sent
Remote files Drag-and-drop uploads and in-place configuration editing
Monitoring Live CPU, memory, disk, and network information
Databases PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, and SQLite
Database operations Browse and edit data, run SQL, import/export dumps, copy databases, and manage users
Automation Saved commands and deployment scripts across one or multiple servers, with retained output
Alerts Telegram and email notifications
Sign-in Email, GitHub, and Google options

Why the SSH-based approach matters

The product describes working without installing an extra agent on your managed servers or opening an additional server port.

For an existing environment, that is a practical design choice: build on the remote access you already maintain.

The database workflow follows the same idea. TermSSH advertises database access through its SSH-based workflow without requiring an additional database port to be opened.

An example workflow

Consider troubleshooting an application after deployment:

  • Select the saved server.
  • Open the terminal and inspect the service.
  • Check CPU and memory usage.
  • Review or edit a remote configuration file.
  • Run a SQL query to investigate application data.
  • Use a saved deployment script for the next rollout.

Those are separate jobs, but they belong to the same investigation. Keeping them in one workspace can make the process easier to follow.

Security features described by the project

The published security policy documents encrypted credential storage using AES-256-GCM, TLS/WSS transport, and TOTP MFA support.

The walkthrough also describes verifying the trusted SSH host key before transmitting credentials.

Try it and share your feedback

TermSSH brings several everyday server-management tools together around an existing SSH connection.

I spent 3–6 November at Devcon 8 in Mumbai as part of the libp2p crew at the Resilient Networking Hub, and I showed Luminar, my GossipSub simulator, to people who work on the real thing.

This was the first Devcon held in India. I came down from a countryside village in Uttarakhand, so for once the biggest Ethereum gathering of the year was a domestic trip for me, not a visa application.

This post covers what the conference was, the talks that set the agenda, what happened at our hub, how the Luminar demo went, and what I am taking home.

The hubs are what made it feel different from a normal conference. Each one was a room run by a community: P2P Networking, Resilient Networking, Security, Privacy, EIP, Agentic, India, Open Source, DeSci, Open Hardware and more. You could spend a whole day in one hub and never see a main stage.

The talks that set the agenda

Five themes ran through the programme: post-quantum migration, privacy by default, a faster L1, agents that pay, and security in the age of AI. Almost every session I can name fits one of them.

The opening keynotes

Day 1's Main Stage block set the tone for the week:

Keynote Speaker
The Open Secure and Verifiable Half to a Brighter Future Vitalik Buterin
Sanctuary, Together Audrey Tang
Post-Quantum Transition Justin Drake, Kev
Reducing the Trust Surface Derek Sorensen, Mooly Sagiv
End-to-End Privacy Nico, Luca Donno

Vitalik's keynote made the case for building technology that is open, secure and verifiable. Later that afternoon he and Audrey Tang took audience questions on civic AI and whether agents can be safe in the open.

Post-quantum is now a roadmap item

Justin Drake and Kev laid out Ethereum's post-quantum transition from the Main Stage, and Drake followed with a full PQ Q&A on Day 2. The topic reached every layer:

  • "Getting to Lean Ethereum" framed the path as two roadmaps that must converge, not one hard fork.
  • The P2P Networking Hub ran "PQ, zk and PQDS: what's the impact on P2P".
  • Our hub ran a workshop on migrating Ethereum's P2P layer to post-quantum cryptography.

For anyone working on libp2p, this is the part to watch. Bigger signatures and new handshakes land on the networking layer first.

A faster, bigger L1

Core Protocol talks were about speed and scale:

  • Glamsterdam. The EIP Hub covered the gas limit going from 60M to 200M and the repricing work behind it.
  • Fast finality. "From 16 Minutes to Seconds" and the Fast Finality update showed decoupled consensus moving from idea to spec.
  • Fast confirmation. The Fast Confirmation Rule targets 13-second confirmations for flows that do not need full finality.
  • FOCIL. Inclusion lists for censorship resistance had lightning talks, an EPF implementation in Lighthouse, and a roundtable at the P2P Networking Hub.

Privacy by default

Privacy & Consent had its own track and a full afternoon on Lotus Stage 1. "Kohaku: privacy for everyone, by default" showed light clients and privacy protocols built into the wallet. "Paths to a Private L1" and "Encrypt the Mempool" pushed the same idea down into the protocol.

Agents that pay

The Agentic Hub ran a packed schedule all four days. x402, ERC-8004 and ERC-8183 came up in almost every slot, and the honest takes were the best ones: registration works, reputation is the hard part, and real usage is smaller than the headlines.

Security in the age of AI

A panel with Vitalik, Mooly Sagiv and others asked how to secure Ethereum when attackers and auditors both have agents. Workshops went hands-on: a prompt-injection lab for AI pipelines, and a Solidity CTF you could enter as a human, a human plus AI, or a fully autonomous agent.

The India angle

ETHIndia's day inside Devcon covered policy, institutions and tokenisation in India. Sandeep Nailwal spoke on open financial rails for the country, and GM Vidit Gujrathi played blindfold chess against two players at once on the ETHIndia stage.

Home base: the Resilient Networking Hub

I spent most of my time at the Resilient Networking Hub, the libp2p-led room that Manu Sheel Gupta put together. I was one of the maintainers on its schedule, and it is the reason I was in Mumbai at all.

The hub asked one question for four days: what makes a network resilient? The sessions answered it from very different angles.

Session Who Angle
Resilient Networks from Zero Manu Sheel Gupta and the hub team Peer identity, discovery, transports, secure connections
What Makes a Network Resilient? Miglė Rakitaitė, Manu Sheel Gupta, Steven Mih and others Research roundtable on connectivity, trust, failure and recovery

Self-Hosted IPFS Infrastructure Anurag Pandey, Manu Sheel Gupta Running and maintaining your own IPFS setup

The hub also took its case to the bigger rooms. Manu and Shouki Tsuda ran "Building Resilient Ethereum" as a workshop on Day 1, and Manu spoke at the Security Hub on security coordination between libp2p and Ethereum infrastructure.

Alongside it, the P2P Networking Hub covered Ethereum's own networking stack: a guided tour by Yiannis Psaras of ProbeLab, Csaba Kiraly of the EF on the mempool and on big blocks with fast diffusion, and Waggle, a hands-on message broadcasting workshop from Sigma Prime. Between the two rooms, networking had a full four-day programme of its own.

I also had few talks with Steven Mih, as well as Kazuma, Ryosuke on what they think of my project and how to improve and work better as a proper Protocol researcher.

Showing Luminar

Luminar is a real-time simulator of a GossipSub v1.1 network: simulated libp2p peers, P1–P4 peer scoring, and attacks you inject while it runs. I built it because gossip attacks are invisible until the mesh breaks, and I wanted the mechanism on screen.

  • Live site: luminar-teal.vercel.app
  • Code: github.com/yashksaini-coder/luminar (MIT)

yashksaini-coder / luminar

Real-time P2P network simulator with live visualization of GossipSub, DHT, and fault injection.

Luminar is a real-time simulator of libp2p GossipSub v1.1: 2–500 peers run mesh maintenance, flood publish, IHAVE/IWANT and P1–P4 peer scoring in a trio loop, and a deck.gl map draws every GRAFT, PRUNE and message hop as it happens. You inject the attack (Sybil, eclipse, partition, drop, latency) and watch which ones scoring catches and which it cannot see. Same mechanism as a beacon node, toy constants.

See it

Offline, no backend: http://localhost:3000/reels/sybil-eclipse/?theme=stage&hero=1.

Demo film (52 s, voiced, captions in demo-16x9.vtt): web/public/video/demo-16x9.mp4. It is the real UI filmed frame by frame from a recording, scored from the same script, and rebuilds from a clean checkout: make demo-record && make demo-render (demo/README.md).

Why

Hermes, Xatu and the ProbeLab dashboards record what the real network did; a Shadow or Testground run tells you what a scripted network would do, from logs, after it finishes. Neither lets you…


View on GitHub


What I showed

The demo runs from two recordings: a Sybil and eclipse run, then a partition that heals.

  1. A publish. Fifty peers gossip, and a message lights the mesh hop by hop. It crosses the network in 4.2 hops on average.
  2. A Sybil attack. Five attacker peers graft into honest meshes at T+10.2 s and flood invalid messages. Each invalid message costs ten points of P4. They fall past the prune threshold and are gone by T+11.9 s, two heartbeats later. Delivery holds at 100%.
  3. An eclipse. Silent attackers take every mesh slot around one peer. They send nothing invalid, so P4 never fires. Scoring cannot see it, and the peer is only freed when the fault is cleared.
  4. A partition. The network is cut in half for 20 seconds. Delivery drops to 50%, then the mesh grafts itself back together in 4.5 s.

The eclipse is the part I care about most. It is easy to assume peer scoring catches everything, and watching the score stay flat while a peer is isolated makes the limit obvious.

Honest by design

Luminar runs the same mechanism as mainnet with toy constants, and I say so on the page. Mesh degree is 6 with a one-second heartbeat. Ethereum mainnet runs D 8, a 0.7 s heartbeat, and score thresholds in the thousands. Luminar scores on P1–P4, while a real node adds P5–P7.

There is also a mainnet mode: a map that lights ethPandaOps observer nodes in the order a real block reached them.

How it is built

Layer Stack
Backend Python 3.12, FastAPI, Trio, py-libp2p, NetworkX
Frontend TypeScript, deck.gl (WebGL), d3-force, Vite
Transport One WebSocket, multiplexed at 20 Hz
Replay Recordings play in the browser with no backend

Every run can be recorded and scrubbed, so a talk does not depend on conference wifi. There is a stage mode with a projector theme for exactly this reason.

People

The hallway is the reason to go to a conference in person. Mine was mostly inside one hub, which meant I kept meeting the same people in different sessions until we were no longer strangers.

  • Manu Sheel Gupta, who leads the libp2p work I contribute to and who brought me into the hub.
  • The maintainers I shared the Network Lab with: Daniel Thompson, Shouki Tsuda, Sumanjeet and Soham Bhoir.
  • Steven Mih of Action State, whose sessions on verifiable agent actions and evidence for AI inference from strangers gave me a new problem to think about.

[ADD: anyone else you want to thank or name, and one conversation worth a full paragraph. Remove anyone above who would rather not be named.]

What I am taking home

  • Networking is no longer the quiet layer. Post-quantum signatures, bigger blocks, shorter slots and inclusion lists all put pressure on P2P first. Two full hubs on networking says the ecosystem knows it.
  • Show the mechanism. A demo people can watch beats a slide that tells them. Luminar exists because I could not see what GossipSub scoring was doing, and that turned out to be a common problem.
  • Be honest about the toy. Saying "same mechanism, toy constants" up front made the conversations better, because nobody had to guess what the simulator could and could not prove.
  • Agents need evidence, not just payments. The agent-payment rails are shipping. The harder question, raised at both our hub and the Agentic Hub, is how a third party verifies what an agent actually did.
  • India showed up. ETHIndia, the India Hub, EPF fellows presenting client work, and a crowd of first-time attendees. Devcon coming here lowered the barrier for a lot of builders, me included.

  • Keep hardening the Kademlia DHT in py-libp2p.

Showing Luminar

Luminar is a real-time simulator of a GossipSub v1.1 network: simulated libp2p peers, P1–P4 peer scoring, and attacks you inject while it runs. I built it because gossip attacks are invisible until the mesh breaks, and I wanted the mechanism on screen.

  • Live site: luminar-teal.vercel.app
  • Code: github.com/yashksaini-coder/luminar (MIT)

yashksaini-coder / luminar

Real-time P2P network simulator with live visualization of GossipSub, DHT, and fault injection.

Luminar is a real-time simulator of libp2p GossipSub v1.1: 2–500 peers run mesh maintenance, flood publish, IHAVE/IWANT and P1–P4 peer scoring in a trio loop, and a deck.gl map draws every GRAFT, PRUNE and message hop as it happens. You inject the attack (Sybil, eclipse, partition, drop, latency) and watch which ones scoring catches and which it cannot see. Same mechanism as a beacon node, toy constants.

See it

Offline, no backend: http://localhost:3000/reels/sybil-eclipse/?theme=stage&hero=1.

Demo film (52 s, voiced, captions in demo-16x9.vtt): web/public/video/demo-16x9.mp4. It is the real UI filmed frame by frame from a recording, scored from the same script, and rebuilds from a clean checkout: make demo-record && make demo-render (demo/README.md).

Why

Hermes, Xatu and the ProbeLab dashboards record what the real network did; a Shadow or Testground run tells you what a scripted network would do, from logs, after it finishes. Neither lets you…


View on GitHub


What I showed

The demo runs from two recordings: a Sybil and eclipse run, then a partition that heals.

  1. A publish. Fifty peers gossip, and a message lights the mesh hop by hop. It crosses the network in 4.2 hops on average.
  2. A Sybil attack. Five attacker peers graft into honest meshes at T+10.2 s and flood invalid messages. Each invalid message costs ten points of P4. They fall past the prune threshold and are gone by T+11.9 s, two heartbeats later. Delivery holds at 100%.
  3. An eclipse. Silent attackers take every mesh slot around one peer. They send nothing invalid, so P4 never fires. Scoring cannot see it, and the peer is only freed when the fault is cleared.
  4. A partition. The network is cut in half for 20 seconds. Delivery drops to 50%, then the mesh grafts itself back together in 4.5 s.

The eclipse is the part I care about most. It is easy to assume peer scoring catches everything, and watching the score stay flat while a peer is isolated makes the limit obvious.

Honest by design

Luminar runs the same mechanism as mainnet with toy constants, and I say so on the page. Mesh degree is 6 with a one-second heartbeat. Ethereum mainnet runs D 8, a 0.7 s heartbeat, and score thresholds in the thousands. Luminar scores on P1–P4, while a real node adds P5–P7.

There is also a mainnet mode: a map that lights ethPandaOps observer nodes in the order a real block reached them.

How it is built

Layer Stack
Backend Python 3.12, FastAPI, Trio, py-libp2p, NetworkX
Frontend TypeScript, deck.gl (WebGL), d3-force, Vite
Transport One WebSocket, multiplexed at 20 Hz
Replay Recordings play in the browser with no backend

Every run can be recorded and scrubbed, so a talk does not depend on conference wifi. There is a stage mode with a projector theme for exactly this reason.

People

The hallway is the reason to go to a conference in person. Mine was mostly inside one hub, which meant I kept meeting the same people in different sessions until we were no longer strangers.

  • Manu Sheel Gupta, who leads the libp2p work I contribute to and who brought me into the hub.
  • The maintainers I shared the Network Lab with: Daniel Thompson, Shouki Tsuda, Sumanjeet and Soham Bhoir.
  • Steven Mih of Action State, whose sessions on verifiable agent actions and evidence for AI inference from strangers gave me a new problem to think about.

[ADD: anyone else you want to thank or name, and one conversation worth a full paragraph. Remove anyone above who would rather not be named.]

What I am taking home

  • Networking is no longer the quiet layer. Post-quantum signatures, bigger blocks, shorter slots and inclusion lists all put pressure on P2P first. Two full hubs on networking says the ecosystem knows it.
  • Show the mechanism. A demo people can watch beats a slide that tells them. Luminar exists because I could not see what GossipSub scoring was doing, and that turned out to be a common problem.
  • Be honest about the toy. Saying "same mechanism, toy constants" up front made the conversations better, because nobody had to guess what the simulator could and could not prove.
  • Agents need evidence, not just payments. The agent-payment rails are shipping. The harder question, raised at both our hub and the Agentic Hub, is how a third party verifies what an agent actually did.
  • India showed up. ETHIndia, the India Hub, EPF fellows presenting client work, and a crowd of first-time attendees. Devcon coming here lowered the barrier for a lot of builders, me included.

How to Scrape Google News Headlines and Real Article URLs

Google News is still one of the fastest ways to see what is being written about a topic, a company or a person, across languages and countries. The painful part is the links: many scrapers leave you with Google redirect URLs instead of the publisher's article. This guide shows how to scrape Google News search results, topics and top stories, and keep the real article URL.

You will use the Google News Scraper on Apify. It covers keyword search, topic headlines and top stories in 47 country and language editions, and can resolve Google redirects to the publisher's own URL. You also get the title, publisher, date and related coverage.

By the end of this article you will have a CSV or JSON file on your machine, and a short Python snippet you can rerun or schedule. The same Actor is also callable from JavaScript and from AI agents through the Apify MCP server.

What you need

  • An Apify account. The Free plan is enough to try a small run.
  • A list of inputs for the Actor (URLs, IDs or search terms — details in the steps below).
  • Optional: Python 3 with the apify-client package if you want to automate the run.

No Google login and no proxy setup are required for normal use. Think of it as a small Google News API you do not have to maintain.

How to run it in the Apify Console

Step 1: Open the Actor

Open https://apify.com/veenkes/veenkes-google-news and click Try for free.

Step 2: Enter queries or topics

A search query such as artificial intelligence is enough. You can also add topic pages. Pick an edition such as US:en, GB:en, DE:de or JP:ja.

Step 3: Set a time range

Use a rolling window (for example the last 7 days) or explicit dates. Keep max items per query small on the first run, and leave URL resolution on if you want publisher links.

Step 4: Export

Start the run and download CSV or JSON. De-duplication can drop the same article if several queries return it.

Time range applies to search queries. URL resolution is the difference between a redirect and a link you can fetch or open directly.

How to run it from Python

Install the official client and call the Actor by its Store id veenkes/veenkes-google-news. Replace YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN with a token from Apify Console > Integrations. Do not commit the token to a public repository.

What to use the data for

Media-monitoring teams watch brand and competitor names in several editions. Researchers build a headline corpus for a topic. AI briefing agents need a short list of recent stories with working URLs. A scheduled hourly or daily run is a simple news radar.

Pricing

Pay-per-result pricing starts at $2.00 per 1,000 articles on the Apify Free plan, with lower unit prices on paid Apify plans, plus a small per-run start fee. Scheduling and automations

In the Apify Console you can schedule the Actor (daily or hourly) and leave the same input in place. When a run finishes you can send a webhook, or connect the Actor in Zapier, Make or n8n. AI agents can discover and call veenkes/veenkes-google-news through Apify's MCP server using the same input.

Good practices and limits

This is not an official Google News API, and the Actor is not affiliated with Google. Headlines and snippets belong to their publishers; use them for monitoring and research rather than republishing a news site. Resolved URLs still point at the publisher, who may have their own access rules.

If a run returns fewer rows than you expected, check the input caps, language or country filters, and the Actor log. A zero-row run is usually a filter or an unavailable source, not a silent crash — read the log before you increase limits.

Frontend.title: Scrape Property Finder Data with Python: What Furniture Adds to a Dubai Rent
Frontend.summary:
A furnished 1-bedroom apartment in Al Barsha listed on Property Finder this week asks a median AED 85,000 a year. An unfurnished one asks AED 65,000. That is 30.8% more for a sofa, a bed and a fridge, and it is the largest gap I found for 1-bedroom flats in ten Dubai areas.

Tenants moving to Dubai ask the same question every year: is it cheaper to rent unfurnished and buy the furniture? Landlords ask the mirror question: does furnishing a flat pay? Both start with one number, the premium a furnished flat commands over an unfurnished one in the same area. Property Finder has a furnishing filter, so I pulled both sides with Python and compared them. The median premium across the ten areas is 11.3% for 1-bedroom flats and 12.5% for 2-bedroom flats. The bigger lesson is in Dubai Hills Estate, where furnished flats look cheaper and are not.

The data

Every listing here was pulled through the Property Finder API. Its /search-rent endpoint takes a furnishing parameter (furnished, unfurnished or partly), so the split costs nothing extra: one call per area, bedroom count and furnishing state.

On 4 November 2026 I made 40 calls: ten areas, 1- and 2-bedroom apartments, furnished and unfurnished, the first page of yearly rentals sorted by newest. That returned 1,465 rows. After dropping project cards and a few broken rows (more on both below), 1,307 listings were left, about 33 per area, bedroom count and furnishing state. Each response also carries total_count, the number of matching listings on the site, which shows how much of each market is furnished: 15,800 furnished against 16,920 unfurnished listings in these twenty segments.

The ten areas fall into three groups: the waterfront (Dubai Marina, Emaar Beachfront, Palm Jumeirah), the central towers (Downtown Dubai, Business Bay, Jumeirah Lake Towers or JLT) and the suburbs (Jumeirah Village Circle or JVC, Dubai Hills Estate, Al Barsha, Dubai Silicon Oasis). /autocomplete-location turns each name into a location ID.

The code

This is the whole comparison for one area and bedroom count. Install requests, set the RAPIDAPI_KEY environment variable to your RapidAPI key, and run it.

import json
import os
import statistics

import requests

HOST = "uae-real-estate-property.p.rapidapi.com"  # Property Finder API on RapidAPI
BASE = os.environ.get("API_BASE", "https://" + HOST)


def headers():
    if "API_BASE" in os.environ:
        return json.loads(os.environ.get("API_HEADERS", "{}"))
    return {"x-rapidapi-host": HOST, "x-rapidapi-key": os.environ["RAPIDAPI_KEY"]}


def get(path, **params):
    r = requests.get(BASE + path, params=params, headers=headers(), timeout=120)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()


def location_id(name):
    found = get("/autocomplete-location", query=name)["data"]
    exact = [x for x in found if x["name"].lower() == name.lower()]
    return (exact or found)[0]["id"]


def rents(loc, bedrooms, furnishing):
    """Newest yearly rents for one furnishing state: (rent, size in sq ft) pairs, and the total count."""
    body = get("/search-rent", location_id=loc, property_type="apartment", bedrooms=bedrooms,
               rent_frequency="yearly", furnishing=furnishing, sort="newest", page=1)
    rows = []
    for x in body["data"]:
        price, size = x.get("price") or {}, (x.get("size") or {}).get("value")
        # Skip new-project cards (sale prices), non-yearly prices and rows with no size
        if (x.get("listing_type") != "property" or not price.get("value")
                or price.get("period") != "yearly" or not size):
            continue
        if price["value"] / size > 1000:  # a sale price, or a size typed in square metres
            continue
        rows.append((price["value"], size))
    return rows, body["total_count"]


area, beds = "Jumeirah Lake Towers", 1
loc = location_id(area)
furn, furn_total = rents(loc, beds, "furnished")
unfurn, unfurn_total = rents(loc, beds, "unfurnished")

for name, rows in (("furnished", furn), ("unfurnished", unfurn)):
    print("%-12s %2d listings, median AED %s a year, AED %.0f per sq ft" % (
        name, len(rows), format(statistics.median(r for r, s in rows), ",.0f"),
        statistics.median(r / s for r, s in rows)))

premium = statistics.median(r for r, s in furn) / statistics.median(r for r, s in unfurn) - 1
premium_psf = statistics.median(r / s for r, s in furn) / statistics.median(r / s for r, s in unfurn) - 1
print("furniture premium: %+.1f%% on the median rent, %+.1f%% per sq ft" % (premium * 100, premium_psf * 100))
print("furnished share of listings: %.0f%%" % (100 * furn_total / (furn_total + unfurn_total)))

For a 1-bedroom in JLT it printed:

furnished    33 listings, median AED 95,000 a year, AED 110 per sq ft
unfurnished  33 listings, median AED 79,999 a year, AED 101 per sq ft
furniture premium: +18.8% on the median rent, +8.9% per sq ft
furnished share of listings: 58%

The API_BASE switch is there so the same script can point at a test server; with only RAPIDAPI_KEY set it calls RapidAPI. The full version loops over the ten areas, caches every response and also compares listings building by building. Two numbers come out of every pair, and you need both: the premium on the median rent and the premium per square foot.

Furnished flats ask about 11% more

For 1-bedroom apartments, furnished listings ask more than unfurnished ones in 7 of the 10 areas. The median premium is 11.3%.

Al Barsha leads at 30.8%, then Downtown Dubai at 25.0% (AED 150,000 furnished against AED 119,999) and JLT at 18.8%. Business Bay shows no premium at all: both sides have a median of AED 90,000. Palm Jumeirah furnished 1-beds ask 3.1% less, and Dubai Hills Estate 12.7% less.

For 2-bedroom flats the median premium is 12.5%, and furnished asks more in 9 of 10 areas. Downtown Dubai stands out again at 33.3%: AED 220,000 against AED 165,000. Dubai Silicon Oasis shows 64.7%, but only 24 furnished 2-bedroom flats were listed there in total, and they are much bigger than the unfurnished ones (a median of 1,501 sq ft against 1,082). That is a sample to note, not a finding.

In money, the premium is easy to read. A furnished 1-bed in JVC asks AED 8,000 a year more than an unfurnished one; in JLT the gap is AED 15,001, and in Downtown Dubai about AED 30,000. That Downtown figure compares different buildings, though: in the 6 Downtown buildings with both kinds of 1-bed listing, the median furnished flat asked 13.5% less than the unfurnished one. Whether that beats buying your own furniture depends on how long you stay, but it is a yearly cost, paid again at every renewal.

Divide by the size and every gap turns positive

Dubai Hills Estate was the result that made me look twice. On the median rent, furnished flats there are 12.7% cheaper for 1-bedrooms and 21.9% cheaper for 2-bedrooms. That would make it the one area where landlords pay you to take their furniture.

They don't. The furnished flats in Dubai Hills are smaller. The median furnished 1-bed is 645 sq ft against 743 sq ft unfurnished, and the median furnished 2-bed is 748 sq ft against 1,118. My reading is that the compact 2-bedroom units are the ones landlords furnish, while the large family layouts are let empty. Per square foot, furnished flats in Dubai Hills ask 16.2% more for 1-bedrooms and 14.7% more for 2-bedrooms.

The same thing happens on Palm Jumeirah, where furnished 1-beds look 3.1% cheaper and are 4.1% dearer per square foot. Measured per square foot, furnished flats ask more in all 20 area and bedroom pairs. The median premium per square foot is 12.6% for 1-bedrooms and 16.9% for 2-bedrooms.

Per square foot is still not a perfect control, because a furnished flat can sit in a newer or better building. So I also matched listings building by building. In 132 cases the same building had both furnished and unfurnished listings in my sample. Comparing the medians inside each building, furnished asked more in 91 of them (69%), and the median premium was 9.6%: 6.5% for 1-bedrooms and 13.6% for 2-bedrooms. That is the cleanest estimate here, and it is a little lower than the area figures, which suggests part of the area premium is the building, not the furniture.

How common furnished flats are does not set the premium

The total_count field gives the share of each market that is furnished, and it varies more than the premium does.

Downtown Dubai (67.9%), Palm Jumeirah (65.7%) and Emaar Beachfront (64.4%) list most 1-beds furnished. My guess is that they draw more short stays and new arrivals, though this data cannot show it. At the other end, only 19.9% of 1-bed rentals in Al Barsha and 12.6% in Dubai Silicon Oasis are furnished.

It would be neat if scarcity set the price, but the data does not say so. Al Barsha has one of the smallest furnished shares and the largest 1-bed premium, 30.8%. Dubai Hills Estate is mostly unfurnished too (23.7% furnished), and its furnished 1-beds ask 12.7% less, because they are smaller. Dubai Silicon Oasis, where furnished is rarest, asks only 4.8% more. And in Downtown, where furnished is the norm, the area median still shows 25.0% more for a 1-bed, perhaps because furnished Downtown flats are often serviced units in branded towers, even though the same-building comparison above points the other way. Across all twenty segments, 48.3% of the listings are furnished.

Pitfalls I hit in the listings

Project cards ignore the filter. 154 of the 1,465 rows were new-project cards (listing_type is project), with a "from" sale price instead of a yearly rent. 77 of them were identical in the furnished and unfurnished results for the same search, so the furnishing filter does not apply to them. Keep only listing_type == "property" with a price.value and price.period == "yearly".

Some rents are not rents. One unfurnished 1-bed in Dubai Hills Estate was listed at AED 4,000,000 a year for 757 sq ft, which is a sale price in the wrong box. Two others had sizes of 11 and 135 sq ft, most likely square metres typed as square feet. A ceiling of AED 1,000 per sq ft a year removes all three and nothing else. The median barely notices them; an average does.

The median rent hides the size mix. This is the Dubai Hills lesson. Before you report a furnished premium for an area, check the median size on both sides. If they differ by more than a few percent, report the rent per square foot too.

There is a third option. Property Finder also has furnishing=partly. I left it out, so the furnished share above is furnished against unfurnished only, not against the whole market.

"Newest" can reach back months. Where a segment is small, the first page of the newest listings is most of the segment. The oldest listing in my sample was posted on 20 May 2026. In Dubai Silicon Oasis the 24 furnished 2-beds are the whole furnished market for that size, not a sample of it.

Asking is not signed. All of these are asking rents. The registered lease records in /get-transactions do not say whether a flat was furnished, so this data cannot check the premium against signed rents. Treat the figures as what landlords ask for furniture, not what tenants end up paying for it.

Where I would take it next

I would repeat the building match with more pages per segment, so each building has five or more listings on each side, and add furnishing=partly as a middle group. I would also track the same buildings over a few months: if furnished listings stay on the market longer, the premium is partly wishful.

For the signed-rent side of these areas, the Al Barsha rent page and the Dubai Hills Estate rent page on UAEPropertyAPI show median lease rents by bedroom count, updated monthly. The parameters used here are documented in the Happy Endpoint reference for the Property Finder API, more Python and JavaScript examples sit in the GitHub repo, and a key is a sign-up away on RapidAPI. For every Property Finder listing with its price changes as one file, see the listings dataset, or contact us for something custom.

Introduction: The CI/CD Imperative

In today's fast-paced software development landscape, Continuous Integration (CI) and Continuous Deployment (CD) are no longer optional luxuries but fundamental necessities. They empower development teams to deliver code changes more frequently and reliably, significantly accelerating the software development lifecycle. At its core, CI/CD is about automating the build, test, and deployment processes, allowing developers to focus on writing great code rather than getting bogged down in manual, error-prone tasks. This article will guide you through setting up a robust CI/CD pipeline using GitHub Actions, a powerful and flexible automation platform integrated directly into GitHub.

Why GitHub Actions?

GitHub Actions provides a seamless way to automate your workflows, from building and testing code to deploying applications. Its event-driven nature means that actions can be triggered by a wide range of GitHub events, such as pushing code, creating pull requests, or even scheduling tasks. The platform offers a rich marketplace of pre-built actions, allowing you to integrate with various services and tools without reinventing the wheel. This level of integration and extensibility makes it an ideal choice for modern development teams looking to streamline their operations. For businesses seeking to understand market dynamics, evaluating the success of such development practices can sometimes be compared to understanding the landscape of industries like real estate. For instance, understanding the factors that make Top Real Estate Companies in Delhi NCR successful involves analyzing their operational efficiency and market responsiveness, much like how CI/CD impacts software delivery.

Setting Up Your First CI/CD Pipeline

Let's walk through creating a basic CI/CD pipeline for a simple Node.js application. This pipeline will automatically build and test your code whenever changes are pushed to the repository.

1. Create a Workflow File

Navigate to your GitHub repository and create a directory named .github/workflows in the root of your project. Inside this directory, create a YAML file, for example, ci.yml.

2. Define the Workflow

Here's a sample ci.yml file:

name: CI Pipeline

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]
  pull_request:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build-and-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Use Node.js 18.x
        uses: actions/setup-node@v3
        with:
          node-version: '18.x'
      - name: Install Dependencies
        run: npm ci
      - name: Run Tests
        run: npm test

Explanation:

  • name: The name of your workflow.
  • on: Defines the events that trigger the workflow (push and pull request to the main branch).
  • jobs: Contains one or more jobs that will run.
  • build-and-test: The ID of our job.
  • runs-on: Specifies the runner environment (Ubuntu latest).
  • steps: A sequence of tasks to execute.
    • actions/checkout@v3: Checks out your repository code.
    • actions/setup-node@v3: Sets up the Node.js environment.
    • npm ci and npm test: Commands to install dependencies and run tests.

3. Adding Deployment (CD)

To add deployment, you would extend this workflow. For example, you could add a deploy job that runs after build-and-test completes successfully. This might involve using actions to deploy to cloud providers like AWS, Azure, or Vercel.

# ... (previous steps)

  deploy:
    needs: build-and-test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' # Only deploy from main branch
    steps:
      - name: Deploy to Production
        run: echo "Deploying to production..."
        # Add your actual deployment script here

Conclusion

GitHub Actions offers a powerful, integrated solution for implementing CI/CD pipelines. By automating your build, test, and deployment processes, you can significantly improve development velocity and code quality. The flexibility and extensive marketplace of actions allow for customization to fit almost any project's needs. Embracing CI/CD with tools like GitHub Actions is a critical step towards modern, efficient software development.

DevOps.title: Unlocking Cloud Native: A Deep Dive into Kubernetes & Microservices
DevOps.summary:
Introduction: The Microservices Revolution

The software development landscape has undergone a seismic shift. Gone are the days of monolithic applications, slowly being replaced by the agility and scalability offered by microservices. This architectural style breaks down complex applications into smaller, independent services, each responsible for a specific business capability. This approach fosters faster development cycles, improved fault isolation, and the ability to scale individual components. However, managing a distributed system of this nature presents unique challenges.

Orchestrating Complexity: The Role of Kubernetes

This is where Kubernetes (K8s) emerges as a game-changer. As the de facto standard for container orchestration, Kubernetes automates the deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications. It provides a robust framework for handling the intricacies of microservices, abstracting away much of the underlying infrastructure complexity.

Core Kubernetes Concepts for Microservices:

  • Pods: The smallest deployable units in Kubernetes, typically encapsulating one or more containers that share resources. For microservices, a pod often runs a single service container.
  • Deployments: Manage the lifecycle of Pods, enabling declarative updates and rollbacks. This is crucial for zero-downtime deployments of microservices.
  • Services: Provide a stable network endpoint for a set of Pods, abstracting away the dynamic nature of Pod IPs. This allows other services to discover and communicate with your microservices reliably.
  • Ingress: Manages external access to services within the cluster, often handling HTTP and HTTPS routing, SSL termination, and name-based virtual hosting. Essential for exposing your microservices to the outside world.
  • ConfigMaps & Secrets: Allow for the decoupling of configuration data and sensitive information from container images, promoting better security and manageability.

Building Resilient Microservices with K8s

Kubernetes inherently provides several features that contribute to building resilient microservices. Its self-healing capabilities automatically restart failed containers, reschedule pods on healthy nodes, and replace terminated pods. Health checks (liveness and readiness probes) ensure that traffic is only sent to healthy instances of your services. Furthermore, Kubernetes' declarative nature means you define the desired state, and the system works to maintain it, providing a strong foundation for distributed systems. This is particularly important when considering complex deployments, much like navigating the diverse offerings from Top Real Estate Companies in Delhi NCR requires careful planning and execution.

Beyond the Basics: Advanced Patterns

As your microservices architecture matures, you'll encounter more advanced patterns that Kubernetes can help implement:

  • Service Mesh (e.g., Istio, Linkerd): Provides advanced traffic management, observability, and security features at the platform level, independent of application code.
  • CI/CD Pipelines: Integrating Kubernetes with CI/CD tools (like Jenkins, GitLab CI, Argo CD) automates the build, test, and deployment process for your microservices.
  • Observability: Leveraging tools like Prometheus for metrics, Grafana for visualization, and Elasticsearch/Fluentd/Kibana (EFK) for logging is critical for understanding the behavior of your distributed system.

Conclusion: Embracing the Cloud Native Future

Kubernetes has become indispensable for organizations adopting microservices. By understanding and leveraging its core concepts and advanced features, developers can build, deploy, and manage scalable, resilient, and observable microservice-based applications. The journey into cloud-native development is ongoing, but with Kubernetes as a powerful ally, the path to modern, agile software delivery is clearer than ever.

Kubernetes.title: Unlocking Cloud Native: A Deep Dive into Kubernetes & Microservices
Kubernetes.summary:
Introduction: The Microservices Revolution

The software development landscape has undergone a seismic shift. Gone are the days of monolithic applications, slowly being replaced by the agility and scalability offered by microservices. This architectural style breaks down complex applications into smaller, independent services, each responsible for a specific business capability. This approach fosters faster development cycles, improved fault isolation, and the ability to scale individual components. However, managing a distributed system of this nature presents unique challenges.

Orchestrating Complexity: The Role of Kubernetes

This is where Kubernetes (K8s) emerges as a game-changer. As the de facto standard for container orchestration, Kubernetes automates the deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications. It provides a robust framework for handling the intricacies of microservices, abstracting away much of the underlying infrastructure complexity.

Core Kubernetes Concepts for Microservices:

  • Pods: The smallest deployable units in Kubernetes, typically encapsulating one or more containers that share resources. For microservices, a pod often runs a single service container.
  • Deployments: Manage the lifecycle of Pods, enabling declarative updates and rollbacks. This is crucial for zero-downtime deployments of microservices.
  • Services: Provide a stable network endpoint for a set of Pods, abstracting away the dynamic nature of Pod IPs. This allows other services to discover and communicate with your microservices reliably.
  • Ingress: Manages external access to services within the cluster, often handling HTTP and HTTPS routing, SSL termination, and name-based virtual hosting. Essential for exposing your microservices to the outside world.
  • ConfigMaps & Secrets: Allow for the decoupling of configuration data and sensitive information from container images, promoting better security and manageability.

Building Resilient Microservices with K8s

Kubernetes inherently provides several features that contribute to building resilient microservices. Its self-healing capabilities automatically restart failed containers, reschedule pods on healthy nodes, and replace terminated pods. Health checks (liveness and readiness probes) ensure that traffic is only sent to healthy instances of your services. Furthermore, Kubernetes' declarative nature means you define the desired state, and the system works to maintain it, providing a strong foundation for distributed systems. This is particularly important when considering complex deployments, much like navigating the diverse offerings from Top Real Estate Companies in Delhi NCR requires careful planning and execution.

Beyond the Basics: Advanced Patterns

As your microservices architecture matures, you'll encounter more advanced patterns that Kubernetes can help implement:

  • Service Mesh (e.g., Istio, Linkerd): Provides advanced traffic management, observability, and security features at the platform level, independent of application code.
  • CI/CD Pipelines: Integrating Kubernetes with CI/CD tools (like Jenkins, GitLab CI, Argo CD) automates the build, test, and deployment process for your microservices.
  • Observability: Leveraging tools like Prometheus for metrics, Grafana for visualization, and Elasticsearch/Fluentd/Kibana (EFK) for logging is critical for understanding the behavior of your distributed system.

Conclusion: Embracing the Cloud Native Future

Kubernetes has become indispensable for organizations adopting microservices. By understanding and leveraging its core concepts and advanced features, developers can build, deploy, and manage scalable, resilient, and observable microservice-based applications. The journey into cloud-native development is ongoing, but with Kubernetes as a powerful ally, the path to modern, agile software delivery is clearer than ever.

Kubernetes.title: Fix OOM Kills and MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED on ClickHouse® Servers
Kubernetes.summary:
Introduction

ClickHouse® servers can experience two types of memory-related failures.

In the first, the Linux Out-Of-Memory (OOM) killer terminates clickhouse-server. The service restarts, and all running queries fail.

In the second, multiple queries fail with MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED (code 241). The error message contains (total), indicating that the entire server has reached its memory limit rather than an individual query exceeding its own limit.

Both failures have the same underlying cause: the server is attempting to use more memory than the host can provide.

In this guide, we'll explain how ClickHouse manages server memory, how to identify the source of memory failures, and how to configure appropriate limits to protect your server.

1. Why Memory Failures Happen

ClickHouse maintains a hard memory limit for the entire server. When a query attempts an allocation that would exceed this limit, the query is stopped.

Two steps determine the server's memory limit.

Step 1: Establishing the Memory Ceiling

At startup, ClickHouse calculates its memory ceiling using the available memory and the setting max_server_memory_usage_to_ram_ratio.

The default value is 0.9, meaning ClickHouse can use up to 90% of the available memory for its server memory limit.

The setting max_server_memory_usage defaults to 0, which means no fixed limit is configured. If you specify a fixed value, ClickHouse uses the lower of that value and the calculated ceiling.

For example, on a host with 13.55 GiB of RAM, setting a fixed limit of 15.63 GiB resulted in the following log message:

Lowered setting 'max_server_memory_usage' to 12.20 GiB because the system has too little memory. The new value was calculated as 13.55 GiB available memory * 0.90 max_server_memory_usage_to_ram_ratio

ClickHouse automatically lowered the configured limit because the host could not support the requested amount.

Step 2: Understanding the Runtime Memory Limit

ClickHouse also uses a background thread called the memory worker to recalculate the hard memory limit while the server is running.

The runtime limit is calculated using:

(resident memory + available system memory) * ratio

The result cannot exceed the previously established ceiling.

When other processes consume memory, the available system memory decreases, and the runtime limit can fall accordingly.

For example:

MemoryWorker: Adjusting total memory hard limit from 5.62 GiB to 5.69 GiB (resident: 364.99 MiB, available: 5.97 GiB, ceiling: 12.20 GiB, ratio: 0.9)

The calculation is approximately:

(0.36 GiB + 5.97 GiB) × 0.9 = 5.69 GiB

Although the ceiling remained at 12.20 GiB, the live limit stayed around 6 GiB because other processes were consuming some of the host's memory.

Why the Safety Margin Matters

The ratio provides a safety margin because ClickHouse's memory tracker does not account for every memory allocation.

In one test, MemoryResident was 940 MiB while TrackedMemory was only 365 MiB. The remaining memory was consumed by the kernel, other services, and allocator overhead.

A sudden memory spike can consume the available margin between memory-worker checks, potentially triggering the Linux OOM killer.

What Happens in Containers?

ClickHouse can read memory limits imposed through cgroups.

For example, after setting MemoryMax=8G with systemd and restarting the server, the log showed:

Changed setting 'max_server_memory_usage' to 7.20 GiB (8.00 GiB available memory * 0.90 max_server_memory_usage_to_ram_ratio)

Without a container memory limit, ClickHouse may see the memory available on the entire host rather than the amount intended for the service.

The setting memory_worker_use_cgroup controls the use of cgroup memory information for runtime memory-limit calculations. However, a test on a host with similar free memory inside and outside the limit does not, by itself, prove the behavior.

Version note: In ClickHouse 26.3.9, memory_worker_dynamic_hard_limit does not exist. The limit remains at the ceiling, making the memory ratio an important protection mechanism.

2. How to Confirm the Problem

Before changing settings, determine whether the operating system killed the process or ClickHouse stopped a query because of its own memory limit.

Step 1: Check for OOM Kills

Run:

sudo dmesg -T | grep -i -E "out of memory|killed process"

You can also inspect kernel logs from the last 24 hours:

sudo journalctl -k --since "24 hours ago" | grep -i -E "out of memory|killed process"

Check when the ClickHouse service last started:

systemctl show clickhouse-server -p ActiveEnterTimestamp

If the service started recently and the kernel logs show that clickhouse-serv was killed, the operating system likely terminated the process due to memory pressure.

The kernel truncates process names to 15 characters, which explains why the process name may appear as clickhouse-serv.

Step 2: Find Server-Level Memory Errors

A ClickHouse server-level memory failure typically appears as MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED with error code 241 and (total) in the message.

For example, this error was observed on ClickHouse 26.8.36:

Code: 241. DB::Exception: (total) memory limit exceeded: would use 6.28 GiB (attempt to allocate chunk of 4.00 GiB), current RSS: 2.23 GiB, maximum: 6.08 GiB. OvercommitTracker decision: Query was selected to stop by OvercommitTracker. Untracked memory across all threads: -6.82 MiB: While executing AggregatingTransform. (MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED)

The maximum value represents the live server memory limit. It may be lower than the configured ceiling.

To find recent server-level memory errors, query system.query_log:

SELECT
    event_time,
    query_id,
    substring(exception, 1, 250) AS exception_start
FROM system.query_log
WHERE type = 'ExceptionWhileProcessing'
  AND exception_code = 241
  AND exception LIKE '%(total)%'
  AND event_time > now() - INTERVAL 1 DAY
ORDER BY event_time DESC
LIMIT 20;

The system.errors table contains error counts accumulated since the server started and is reset on restart. The query log provides historical records of individual failures.

Step 3: Compare Process Memory with Host Memory

Run the following query:

SELECT
    metric,
    formatReadableSize(value) AS size
FROM system.asynchronous_metrics
WHERE metric IN (
    'MemoryResident',
    'TrackedMemory',
    'OSMemoryTotal',
    'OSMemoryAvailable'
)
ORDER BY metric;

These metrics help you compare the memory used by ClickHouse with the total and available memory on the host.

Step 4: Read the Live Memory Limit

Use system.server_settings to inspect the current server memory limit:

SELECT
    formatReadableSize(toUInt64(value)) AS live_limit
FROM system.server_settings
WHERE name = 'max_server_memory_usage';

This shows the effective limit, which may differ from the value in your configuration file.

For more information about runtime adjustments, inspect the server logs:

sudo grep -a "Adjusting total memory hard limit" /var/log/clickhouse-server/clickhouse-server.log | tail -5

These messages are available at Trace log level.

3. Understanding the Relevant Settings

The following defaults are based on ClickHouse 26.8.36. Verify them on your own server before making changes.

Run:

SELECT
    name,
    value,
    default,
    changed,
    changeable_without_restart
FROM system.server_settings
WHERE name LIKE 'max_server_memory%'
   OR name LIKE 'memory_worker%';

The important settings are:

Setting Default Purpose Restart required
max_server_memory_usage 0 Defines a fixed server memory limit in bytes. A higher value is lowered to the calculated ceiling. No
max_server_memory_usage_to_ram_ratio 0.9 Controls the share of memory available to the server and determines the memory ceiling. A value of 0 disables the limits established by this ratio. No in the test described
memory_worker_dynamic_hard_limit true Allows the memory worker to recalculate the hard limit at runtime. Yes
memory_worker_use_cgroup true Uses cgroup memory information when calculating the runtime limit. Yes

The changeable_without_restart column may show No for the ratio setting. In the test described here, reloading the configuration still applied the change, and the logs showed a new Changed setting message.

If the expected log message does not appear after reloading the configuration, restart the server.

4. How to Fix Memory Failures

The recommended approach is to reserve memory for the operating system and configure explicit memory limits for containers.

Step 1: Set a Lower Memory Ratio

Create a configuration file at:

/etc/clickhouse-server/config.d/memory.xml

Add the following configuration:


    0.8

A ratio of 0.8 allows ClickHouse to use up to 80% of the available memory for its server memory limit.

For example, on a host with 64 GiB of memory, the ceiling would be 51.2 GiB, leaving 12.8 GiB for the operating system and other processes.

Consider these starting points:

  • 0.8: A reasonable starting point for many hosts.
  • 0.7: Consider this when the host runs other services.
  • 0.85: Consider this only on a dedicated host with carefully monitored memory usage.

These values are starting points, not universal recommendations. The appropriate ratio depends on the host, workload, and memory consumed by other processes.

Reload the configuration:

SYSTEM RELOAD CONFIG;

Then verify the updated setting in the logs:

sudo grep -a "max_server_memory_usage" /var/log/clickhouse-server/clickhouse-server.log | tail -3

You should see a Changed setting message confirming the new value.

For example, a test using a ratio of 0.15 produced:

Changed setting 'max_server_memory_usage' to 2.03 GiB (13.55 GiB available memory * 0.15 max_server_memory_usage_to_ram_ratio)

Configuration tip: Write the new file in a separate directory first, then copy it into config.d/. This reduces the chance of ClickHouse loading a partially written configuration file.

Step 2: Configure a Fixed Memory Limit

If you know how much memory ClickHouse should use on a shared host, you can set an explicit limit alongside the ratio.

Update memory.xml:


    0.8
    53687091200

The value 53687091200 represents 50 GiB in bytes.

A fixed limit makes the memory budget easier to understand and manage. ClickHouse uses the lowest applicable value among the fixed limit, the calculated ceiling, and the runtime limit.

Reload the configuration:

SYSTEM RELOAD CONFIG;

In the test described here, changing the configured value from 3 GiB to 2 GiB through a configuration reload caused the next memory error to report:

maximum: 2.00 GiB

Verify the effective limit in the logs and through system.server_settings.

Step 3: Set a Container Memory Limit

A container memory limit prevents ClickHouse from consuming the entire host's memory.

Docker example:

docker run -d --name clickhouse --memory=32g clickhouse/clickhouse-server

Kubernetes example:

resources:
  requests:
    memory: 32Gi
  limits:
    memory: 32Gi

Setting the Kubernetes memory request equal to the limit reserves the same memory amount for scheduling purposes and helps avoid unexpected memory-pressure evictions caused by overcommitting the requested amount.

With a 32 GiB container limit and a ratio of 0.8, the calculated ceiling is 25.6 GiB.

Systemd's MemoryMax provides a similar cgroup memory limit.

Remember that the container limit and ClickHouse's internal memory limit serve different purposes: the container constrains the process at the operating-system level, while ClickHouse's settings help it stop queries before reaching that boundary.

5. How to Verify the Fix

After changing the configuration, check the effective settings and confirm that the logs show the expected memory limit.

On a test server, you can trigger a memory-limit error using:

SELECT groupArray(number)
FROM numbers(100000000000)
SETTINGS max_memory_usage = 0
FORMAT Null;

Warning: Do not run this test on a production server. It is intended for controlled testing only.

The query should fail with code 241. The maximum value in the error should match the configured effective limit or be lower if the host has insufficient available memory.

For production, monitor the server for seven days after applying the changes.

The fix is working as intended when:

  1. Kernel logs show no new OOM kills.
  2. The query log contains no new unexpected (total) memory-limit errors.
  3. MemoryResident remains below OSMemoryTotal with a safe memory margin.

Continue monitoring workloads that generate large aggregations, memory-intensive queries, merges, and mutations.

6. Risks and Trade-Offs

Lower Limits Can Cause Queries to Fail Earlier

Reducing the memory limit means ClickHouse may reject queries that previously succeeded.

This is often the correct trade-off: a failed query is preferable to a server process being killed and disrupting all running queries.

Identify and tune the heaviest queries rather than simply increasing the server limit.

The Live Limit Can Change

On a shared host, the effective memory limit can decrease when other processes consume more memory.

As a result, queries may fail even when the configured settings have not changed. Investigate other processes and host-level memory usage before increasing ClickHouse's limits.

Merges and Mutations Have Their Own Memory Controls

Merges and mutations have a separate setting:

merges_mutations_memory_usage_to_ram_ratio

Its default is 0.5. Review it when diagnosing memory pressure related to background operations.

Caches Also Consume Memory

Caches contribute to memory consumption. Avoid increasing cache sizes when lowering the server's memory limit unless you have measured the impact and confirmed that sufficient memory remains available.

Be Careful When Using Swap

The setting description notes that low-RAM hosts with swap may require a ratio above 1 in certain situations.

This should only be done deliberately. Allowing ClickHouse to use swap before reaching its configured limit may delay an OOM event, but heavy swapping can make queries extremely slow and postpone rather than prevent a more severe failure.

For ClickHouse hosts, consider disabling swap or configuring a low vm.swappiness value according to your operational requirements.

7. Summary

When troubleshooting ClickHouse memory failures:

  • Check dmesg and the service start time to determine whether the operating system killed the process.
  • Look for MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED code 241 errors containing (total) to identify server-level memory failures.
  • Read the maximum value in the error message to understand the effective live limit.
  • Remember that the live limit is constrained by the fixed limit, the ratio-based ceiling, and the runtime limit calculated by the memory worker.
  • Configure a suitable max_server_memory_usage_to_ram_ratio in config.d/ and reload the configuration.
  • Set an explicit container memory limit when running ClickHouse in Docker, Kubernetes, or another cgroup-managed environment.
  • Monitor kernel logs, query errors, and memory metrics after applying the fix.

The goal is not to let ClickHouse consume every available byte of memory. It is to establish a predictable memory budget that protects the server while allowing normal workloads to run reliably.

References

  • ClickHouse documentation: max_server_memory_usage and max_server_memory_usage_to_ram_ratio.

Kubernetes.title: How to Model an Insurance Policy Without Joining Dozens of Tables
Kubernetes.summary:
Ask an underwriter to describe a policy, and you’ll get a coherent answer: A contract, for a customer, covering a car or a house, with a handful of coverages, each with a limit and a deductible, plus a history of every change since it was issued. One policy—with parts. Many parts.

Now ask your database the same question. In most insurance core systems, that single policy is sliced across dozens of relational tables: one each for coverages, vehicles, named parties, endorsements, and billing schedules. Every time a screen loads, the system reassembles the policy by joining those tables back together. Every time a product changes, several of the tables need altering. When Manulife(1) rebuilt its policy servicing platform, its chief architect described replacing more than 500 core tables with one document per policy and reported that the new system won overwhelming approval from its developers.

That gap—between how the business thinks about a policy and how the database stores it—is the central problem a document database like MongoDB solves. This blog post explains the one design decision that matters most when you make that move and why it’s an insurance decision as much as a technical one.

One rule drives everything

A document database stores records as nested structures, closer to a folder than a spreadsheet row. A policy document can hold its coverages, its vehicles, its parties, and its event history all within itself. The temptation is to simply pour the old table diagram into this new shape. That’s the wrong instinct.

The core idea is to model the data around what the business does with it, not around how the entities look on a diagram. Concretely, that means designing for the policy lifecycle (quote, underwrite, issue, bill, endorse, renew, cancel, claim) and asking, at each step, what gets read and written together.

Once you ask that question, every design choice reduces to one decision: whether to embed or reference.

Embed or reference: The decision that matters

For any two related pieces of data, you have two options. Embed one inside the other, so they live in a single document. Or reference one from the other, storing just an identifier that points to a separate document, the way a relational foreign key does.

The test can be reduced to two very simple statements:

  • Embed data that is part of something and is always read alongside it.

  • Reference data that has its own lifecycle or is shared across many records.

Apply that to a policy and the answers fall out naturally. Coverages belong inside the policy. Nobody ever looks up collision coverage without the policy it sits within. The insured vehicle belongs inside the policy—as does the event history, because an endorsement or a cancellation is meaningless apart from the contract it changed. In document form, that looks like this:

Anyone in the business can read that. It looks like the policy.

The claim follows the same logic, with a payoff that finance teams will appreciate. A claim’s reserves and payments belong inside the claim document. Because a single document is always written atomically, posting a reserve and updating the claim’s total becomes one operation that either fully succeeds or doesn’t happen at all. There’s no window where the ledger and the claim disagree.

Now let’s look at the other side of the test. A customer’s policies should not be embedded inside the customer record. Policies are large, they change constantly, and they’re almost always looked up by policy number rather than through the customer record. Instead, store policies in their own collection and have each policy reference its customer by ID. Claims should not be embedded inside policies either, because a claim can outlive the policy that spawned it: a canceled policy can still have open claims. Store claims separately, with each claim referencing the policy it belongs to.

The agent who sold the policy and the product it was written on should also be referenced, not embedded, and here the reasoning is operational. Thousands of policies share one agent and one product. Embed the agent’s details, and a change to their license number becomes a write across every policy in their book. Keep the product catalog as the single, versioned source of truth, and let the policy store only a point-in-time snapshot of the coverage terms it was bound against.

Two storms that test the design

Insurance also stress-tests data models in a way few other industries do: catastrophes.

The hurricane claim

Most auto and property claims carry fewer than 10 supporting attachments (photos, estimates, or a police report, for example). Embedding them in the claim is fine. But a major-loss claim after a hurricane can accumulate 60 or more attachments. MongoDB has a hard 16 MB size limit per document, but even well below that, a bloated minority of claims slows down every screen that loads them.

The wrong fix is to move all claim documents into a separate collection “just in case,” penalizing the 99% for the 1%. The right fix is what MongoDB’s engineers call the outlier pattern: embed by default, and when a claim crosses a threshold, flip an overflow flag and store the excess in a side collection. The design serves the common case and handles the exception explicitly.

Here’s what that looks like for a hurricane claim. Once the claim crosses the threshold, the application sets the flag and moves the extra documents to the side collection, so the claim record stays small:

The wildfire intake surge

When a database outgrows one server, MongoDB splits it across several, and a field called the shard key decides which server each record lands on. It seems sensible to shard claims by catastrophe (CAT) event code, since the CAT dashboard queries by it. It’s a trap. During an active wildfire, nearly every new claim for days shares one CAT code, so every new claim routes to one server—precisely when intake throughput matters most. Use a hashed shard key on the claim number to spread new claims evenly, and keep the CAT code as an ordinary index for the dashboard.

Both examples carry the same lesson: The data model is where operational resilience is decided, long before the storm arrives.

Three patterns to adopt on day one

Beyond the embed-versus-reference rule, there are three more design patterns to adopt:

  1. Computed totals. Store “total incurred” and “total paid” on the claim rather than re-summing reserves and payments on every read. Claim detail is among the busiest screens in the company; don’t make it do math.

  2. Schema versioning. Stamp every policy and claim with a version number. Insurance records survive for decades under regulatory retention and litigation discovery, and your document shape will change over that time. Without a version marker, that drift becomes an audit problem, not just a technical one. Travelers Insurance(2) is reported to have eliminated a three-day wait for schema changes after moving off a rigid relational model; versioning is what makes that agility safe.

  3. Append-only history. Policy events, claim activity, and increasingly, the step-by-step decision trace of any automated underwriting or fraud-screening agent should only ever be added to, never edited or deleted. In most industries, that’s good hygiene. In insurance, it’s compliance. As regulators turn their attention to AI-driven decisions, an auditable trace of what an automated system decided and why will be the difference between a quick review and a drawn-out one.

What this means for you

None of this requires your engineers to abandon what they know. Multi-document transactions still exist for the moments that need them, such as binding a submission into a policy. The shift is in the starting question. Instead of “What are the entities and how do they relate?” it becomes, “What does the business read and write together, and what changes on its own?”

Keep what’s always read together, well, together. Separate what lives its own life. Plan explicitly for the outlier and the surge. Get those right, and the database finally describes a policy the way your underwriters do.

References: 1. Why Leading Insurer Manulife Ditched SQL For MongoDB 2. Travelers Insurance speeds up business ask-to-production process with MongoDB

Rust.title: TermSSH: SSH, Files, Monitoring, and Databases in One Browser Workspace
Rust.summary:
TermSSH: SSH, Files, Monitoring, and Databases in One Browser Workspace

If you manage remote servers, your workflow probably looks something like this:

  1. Open an SSH session.
  2. Check the application service.
  3. Read the logs.
  4. Edit a configuration file.
  5. Inspect resource usage.
  6. Open a database client.
  7. Repeat on staging.

TermSSH brings these tasks into a shared browser workspace, using the SSH access you already have.

The website calls the application Secure Console, and its public walkthrough covers much more than an embedded terminal.

What’s inside?

Area Advertised capabilities
SSH terminal Full browser shell, keyboard and colour support, sessions that continue across pages, automatic reconnection
Server connections Saved servers and trusted host-key checking before credentials are sent
Remote files Drag-and-drop uploads and in-place configuration editing
Monitoring Live CPU, memory, disk, and network information
Databases PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, and SQLite
Database operations Browse and edit data, run SQL, import/export dumps, copy databases, and manage users
Automation Saved commands and deployment scripts across one or multiple servers, with retained output
Alerts Telegram and email notifications
Sign-in Email, GitHub, and Google options

Why the SSH-based approach matters

The product describes working without installing an extra agent on your managed servers or opening an additional server port.

For an existing environment, that is a practical design choice: build on the remote access you already maintain.

The database workflow follows the same idea. TermSSH advertises database access through its SSH-based workflow without requiring an additional database port to be opened.

An example workflow

Consider troubleshooting an application after deployment:

  • Select the saved server.
  • Open the terminal and inspect the service.
  • Check CPU and memory usage.
  • Review or edit a remote configuration file.
  • Run a SQL query to investigate application data.
  • Use a saved deployment script for the next rollout.

Those are separate jobs, but they belong to the same investigation. Keeping them in one workspace can make the process easier to follow.

Security features described by the project

The published security policy documents encrypted credential storage using AES-256-GCM, TLS/WSS transport, and TOTP MFA support.

The walkthrough also describes verifying the trusted SSH host key before transmitting credentials.

Try it and share your feedback

TermSSH brings several everyday server-management tools together around an existing SSH connection.

If you spend your day moving between terminals, remote files, monitoring, and database clients, take a look:

Explore TermSSH →

Which feature would make the biggest difference to your workflow? What would you want added next?

Rust.title: Devcon 8 Mumbai: Four Days at Ethereum's Biggest Builder Gathering
Rust.summary:
A little late in sharing this, but I wanted to capture all the details as best as I can.

I spent 3–6 November at Devcon 8 in Mumbai as part of the libp2p crew at the Resilient Networking Hub, and I showed Luminar, my GossipSub simulator, to people who work on the real thing.

This was the first Devcon held in India. I came down from a countryside village in Uttarakhand, so for once the biggest Ethereum gathering of the year was a domestic trip for me, not a visa application.

This post covers what the conference was, the talks that set the agenda, what happened at our hub, how the Luminar demo went, and what I am taking home.

[ADD: one or two lines on how you got there: the journey, first impression of the venue, the moment you got your badge.]

I first arrived on 2 Nov at the venue and connected with some friends of a co-exhibitor of our Hub. It was great to see people with whom I've been working over the past year. Got two different badges: one, a simple Dev Attendee, and another for exhibitors for Hubs who are presenting.

Devcon 8 at a glance

Devcon is the Ethereum Foundation's conference for the people who build the protocol and everything around it. The 2026 edition ran for four days in one venue, the Jio World Centre in Bandra Kurla Complex.
Dates 3–6 November 2026
Venue Jio World Centre, BKC, Mumbai
Programme 928 sessions across main stages and Community Hubs
Busiest days Day 2 and Day 3, 283 sessions each
Tracks 9: Core Protocol, Security, Privacy & Consent, Applied Cryptography, Permissionless Networks, Open & Verifiable Stack, Users/Builders/Agents, Rights/Freedoms/Governance, Futures Worth Building
Community Hubs 18 community-run spaces, each with its own schedule

The hubs are what made it feel different from a normal conference. Each one was a room run by a community: P2P Networking, Resilient Networking, Security, Privacy, EIP, Agentic, India, Open Source, DeSci, Open Hardware and more. You could spend a whole day in one hub and never see a main stage.

The full programme is in the Devcon app, and every session is going up on the Devcon Archive.

Four days, as they happened

I posted from the floor all week. The posts are embedded below in the order I wrote them.

Day 1, Tuesday 3 November: opening and the first Network Lab
